utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. May I remind you, sir, of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies. Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Zirojevic, please tell us in some detail what you were doing 15 years ago today, on the 17th of October, 1991. What you were doing 15 years ago today?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 15 years ago today, I was in the area of the town of Vukovar, the street of Svetozara Markovica. We were carrying out combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: What sort of combat activities were you carrying out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the combat activity of attacking the paramilitary forces of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your answer is very general without detail, Mr. Zirojevic, and yesterday you were giving us answer after answer of a specific date, without any reference to any document, without any reference to any diary, without any reference to any record, and without any hesitation. Now this morning you seemed to hesitate when you were asked the question and you thereafter have given an answer with a very vague general terms. Isn't it the case, Mr. Zirojevic, that your memory is not as good as you want this Court to believe?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not remember the details of every particular day, but I remember some details that remain firmly etched in my memory because they involved either tragic events or happy events. I cannot tell you exactly what I did on the 17th of October 15 years ago. But at any rate, I was engaged in combat activity commanding my unit, and had anything left a special impression on me on that day, of course I would have remembered it. But if I saw with my very own eyes the death of a man who was my friend, of course I'm going to remember that date and that day very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: One of the incidents you remembered yesterday at page 70 in your testimony was the leaving of Major Tesic to go to Belgrade on the evening of the 20th of November, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And your testimony yesterday also at page 70 was that he returned the next day, the 21st of November, 1991; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Zirojevic, this Court has heard evidence at page 12.086 that contrary to your memory, Major Tesic left on the 21st of November, 1991, not the 20th. That he left in the morning, not in the evening. And that he returned on the 22nd, not the 21st of November. Do you accept that you could be wrong about that date?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the evening of the 20th, for about 20 minutes, he was at the regular briefing at the command post and that after that, he said he was going to Negoslavci and from there to Belgrade. Now whether he went on that evening or the following morning, I have no way of knowing that because after the briefing, we first went to the area of disposition of our own units and then to Captain Vuckovic's for dinner. I saw him at the briefing on the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I've understood your answer correctly, Mr. Zirojevic, it's your memory that you saw Major Tesic on the briefing -- at the briefing of the 21st of November, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And if other witnesses have told us he did not return until the 22nd of November, is it they who are wrong or you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what other witnesses said to you. I told you what I know and the way I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Zirojevic, you stayed in the army after Vukovar until 1996; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And I don't need to know any details of what you were doing, but for the five years after Vukovar, you were involved in military operations; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was involved in protecting the state border vis-a-vis the war-torn areas of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And you being a professional soldier, being good enough for the Guards Motorised Brigade, your mind would be on the tasks you were performing at that time when you were protecting those borders; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope so, since there weren't any objections on the part of my superiors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this has nothing to do with the indictment. We clarified this question earlier on before the Court, but I did not understand it to have anything to do with credibility either. So I do not see in which direction my learned friend is taking this cross-examination. If it has nothing to do with the indictment, then I think it's a waste of time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there certainly has been no question with regard to the details of what happened between 1991 and 1996. The witness was asked if he was involved in combat operations and was his mind focused on the job he was doing. It's more a question and a line of questioning with regards to his memory and nothing to do with actual content of where he was and what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, carry on for the moment, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: With you being involved with these other operations between 1991 and 1996 and being focused in that job as you've told us, you would not be constantly thinking about Vukovar and inconsequential dates, would you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already given you an answer, that I did not take part in combat operations. I took part in protecting the state border vis-a-vis the war-torn areas, that is to say that I secured the state border with my unit lest there be any penetration from the areas that were engulfed in a war. That is to say the territory of the federal republic of --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I don't want any details of what activities you were doing, just with regard to your memory. You were not sitting at this border protecting former Yugoslavia trying to remember about stopping the use of messengers on the 10th of -- 10th of October, 1991, you were not sitting during your duties thinking about an order of the 14th of November dividing the 1st Assault Detachment, were you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. But the impressions I have from Vukovar, since that was something quite new and it was the first time in my military career, of course that remains firmly etched in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Zirojevic, when did you first know that you had become a Defence witness?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first heard that I would become a Defence witness at the beginning of July this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: So for 14 and a half years since the fall of Vukovar, you did not know you would have to give evidence on any of these matters; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And when did you first speak to the Defence team about these matters and discuss your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We first spoke about subjects that had to do with this trial in the year when Mr. Radic was detained. It wasn't only me; there were quite a few of us. It was in general terms about everything that was going on in that period in the territory of the town of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And the year in which Mr. Radic was detained, you spoke to a few people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to the team of Mr. Borovic, the Defence team, Mr. Borovic and his associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And during your times in Vukovar, Mr. Zirojevic, you did not keep a diary of any kind, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The company commander was duty-bound to keep a war diary at company level.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You have not answered the question you were asked, Mr. Zirojevic. You, yourself, did not keep any diary, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did keep a war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And what did you do with that war diary at the conclusion of the Vukovar operations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On orders from the battalion commander upon our return to Belgrade, the war diary and all documents related to the operations, all the maps that we drew there, if we drew any, we handed over to the battalion command. That was archived and it is probably in the archives of the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: The diary you're talking about would include information, important information about combat activities, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, everything that is important, that is to say orders, losses, everything that was significant in terms of dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: That diary would not have any record of any dinner held on the 20th of November, 1991, would it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that was not a combat action.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And you, yourself, have no personal diary about what you were doing, never mind professional operational matters and combat activities, but you have no personal diary about what was happening in Vukovar in November 1991, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't have a personal diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And you have no written record whatsoever about this dinner on the 20th of November, 1991, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You have no list of who attended that dinner on 20th of November, 1991, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You have no list of how many people attended that dinner on 20th of November, 1991, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You have no list of when the dinner guests arrived on the 20th of November, 1991, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And Mr. Zirojevic, you have no record of when people left that dinner on the 20th of November, 1991, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Zirojevic, you fought alongside Captain Radic at Vukovar and you're friends with him; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And you are here in The Hague to help your friend; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came here to give my contribution to proving the truth in these proceedings. If that helps my friend, I will be happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: But Mr. Zirojevic, your contribution has gone beyond simply coming here to give your evidence, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I haven't understood your question. Could you please rephrase it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You have gone out of your way, Mr. Zirojevic, to help your friend's Defence team by contacting at least one other Defence witness; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that yet again, I have not understood what your question was. I told the Defence what I know about these events. Now, whether they came to some conclusion on the basis of that and whether they called some other witness on the basis of that, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: But Mr. Zirojevic, not the Defence, but you, you, yourself, called a potential Defence witness and you, yourself, arranged for that person to make contact with Mr. Borovic's Defence team, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: It's your evidence you did not call any other witness and arrange a meeting with Mr. Borovic; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert that that is not correct. Perhaps I got a telephone number or address, but I did not organise a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Zirojevic, I can refresh your memory. This Court has heard evidence at page 12.958 that Slavko Stijakovic received a telephone call from you arranging for him to meet Mr. Borovic. Do you know who Slavko Stijakovic is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know who Slavko Stijakovic is. He was the deputy commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion at the time of the Vukovar operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And if this Court heard evidence that he received a telephone call from you, is the witness who told us that telling a lie or are you telling us a lie?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not like to obstruct, but big words have been addressed to the witness. He was saying what he knows and telling him that he is lying once the witness already said that there was telephone contact, I don't think that such a big word should be used in addressing this witness, and what my learned friend is saying is not correct anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think in testimony the witness has said that he did not make any telephone call, that he may have provided at best a telephone number to Mr. Borovic's office and allowed them to make contact. He has denied twice making any contact directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Lunny, it might be more useful to wonder in your question whether this witness is mistaken or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: That certainly would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That would perhaps will achieve all your purposes if you ask that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I do not think so, with respect. It is the Prosecution's position that the witness is indeed not being truthful on this point, and I am simply putting the Prosecution case to him. It certainly would be open to him to answer "I may be mistaken." But he has not done so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, that is the case you say you wish to put, you should put it. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: This Court has heard evidence, Mr. Zirojevic, that you made a telephone call to Slavko Stijakovic. You are now -- you, rather, are denying making any such phone call. Are you being truthful in that or are you telling a lie?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to explain something to you. Before I give anyone a telephone number, before that, I contact the said person and I ask whether I can disclose their telephone, so that this person would not be disturbed, if he or she doesn't want to be disturbed. Of course before I gave this telephone number to Mr. Borovic I talked to Mr. Stijakovic and I asked him whether I could give his telephone number. I did not say that I had no telephone contacts. I just said that I did not organise the meeting. Now, what Mr. Borovic and Mr. Stijakovic agreed upon after they spoke and where they met up eventually, I do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Zirojevic, you are not changing your testimony midstream; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me if I had organised the meeting. I did not organise it. I told you that I obtained the telephone number. I have just explained to you the way I did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Did you contact any other potential Defence witnesses whilst trying to help your friend's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same way I may have done it with several others. The same way I have just explained to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Who were the several others?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but there (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You've given us one name, Mr. Zirojevic. Were there any others you contacted?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the commander of the military police platoon who was at the time within the 1st Battalion, Predrag Stefanovic, Second Lieutenant; there was the commander of the anti-armour company, Sladjan Kopcic; the commander of the 1st Company, Sasa Bojkovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. I rose too soon, but you do know which the witnesses have protective measures and have to be protected. I wanted to move that we move into closed session whilst mentioning these names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. It may have been a very valuable move but as you will have seen, I have grown concerned about the extent of interruption of questioning at the point which could be critical either to fact or merit, so I'm dealing with that by delaying the interference until the answer is given. This is, I think, the only fair way to all sides. Thank you for thinking of the question of confidentiality. Carry on, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Zirojevic, what about Davor Vuskovic; is that someone you know? Sorry, Vukovic, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- do you mean Davor Vuckovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Davor Vuckovic was the commander of the mortar battery.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And in providing help to your friend's Defence team, did you contact him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: What about Major Tesic? Did you contact Major Tesic to see if he could help your friend's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Major Tesic, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Now, when you contacted all of these men to provide help to your friend's Defence team, you'd have discussed Vukovar, old times, old memories good and bad, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this question has to do with that other question as to whether I gave names and contact numbers to Mr. Borovic, well, I did it the way I just explained. And of course when we met, we would reminisce about the -- those times, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You would reminisce by discussing what your testimony would be in The Hague, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until early July of this year, it was not certain that I would indeed be a witness in these proceedings. I was one of the potential witnesses. It was only in early July, earlier this year, that I was told that I was proposed as a witness and that I would most likely testify in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You have not answered the question you were asked, Mr. Zirojevic. You were at least a potential witness, you were meeting with other potential witnesses. You had fought together in Vukovar in 1991 and you would have discussed, amongst this group, what happened in Vukovar and what your testimony might be if you were called to The Hague; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we reminisced about those times. We did not specifically cast our minds back to certain dates or events. We merely recalled those times and what they involved. We did not go back to any specific events. We talked about matters that remained etched in our memories.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Captain Radic had been called to The Hague. You were meeting with other people from Vukovar, former colleagues. You knew you were a potential witness, you were discussing Vukovar. You knew about Ovcara at that stage and the dates involved, and are you telling this Court that when sitting together you did not cast your mind back to specific dates, for example, the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: Yes, we talked about the matters and events that remained firmest in our memories. We could not recall every single date and every single event, but what was very striking, what remained impressed in our memories, those were the subject of our discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Just before I move on, Mr. Zirojevic, with regard to contacting potential witnesses for your friend's Defence team, did you have the ability to contact Major Tesic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Having that ability, did you contact him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the sense you asked me about the other potential witnesses, no, not in that sense, but I did meet with him on several occasions. But the purpose of our encounters was not the one we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Having that ability and having gone out of your way to find other potential witnesses for your friend's Defence team, why did you not ask Major Tesic for help?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's simply that I think that -- well, I don't know. Either Mr. Borovic did not wish to speak to him or else I don't know why I didn't ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If you just bear with me one moment, Mr. Zirojevic. When you spoke to Major Tesic, did you ask Major Tesic if he was prepared to give evidence on behalf of Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I didn't speak with him about that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I can move on, Mr. Zirojevic. Now by the fall of Vukovar, 18th of November, 1991, you had been fighting for over six weeks; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the 1st of October up until the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And this period was stressful, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the first to the last day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And during that period, having that stress, you wouldn't get much sleep, would you, Mr. Zirojevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one couldn't put it that way. At nightfall, all the activities ceased, positions were organised and fortified and then one could rest. Naturally, there were times when we awoke at night for combat actions but this did not take place every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I think you said yesterday at page 72, Mr. Zirojevic, that by the 20th of November, you were decompressing from all of that stress; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that we were decompressing. I said that from the 20th November on, the very fact that we were in an area where there were no more combat activities, it was only natural for a person to relax and not feel the way one felt before the fall of Vukovar. There were no more threats of attacks from the other side, that is to say from the Croatian paramilitary forces. It was not time of peace, but it was time of semi-peace. We were still in an area of combat but the threat to one's person and soldiers was not high.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Now, this period at the end of November 1991, the 20th of November to be specific, it's late November and it's cold outside, isn't it, Mr. Zirojevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And we've heard evidence, Mr. Zirojevic, at page 12.665 that the house where you had the dinner hadn't been finished being built yet; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by the fact that it was not finished. Well, it wasn't finished in terms of the fact that it hadn't been plastered on the outside. There was no facade. You could see the bricks. But for the rest, the house was finished. The men lived in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Zirojevic, this dinner didn't last all night until dawn, did it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dinner lasted deep into the night, yes, almost until dawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Captain Radic left this dinner early and went back to Nova Ulica 81 certainly before 1.00 a.m. and perhaps even earlier, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. We left together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was waiting for the answer. I waited for the answer to come. I would appeal to my learned friend to treat the witness properly. Captain Radic never stated that. He said that it was just up until dawn, that it was quite chilly, and this is the way it should be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But I don't think Mr. Lunny is putting evidence of your client, Mr. Borovic, if you've look closely at his questions. He is putting a situation, a set of facts. On what they're based, I don't know. Yes, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite correct. Your Honour, I'm putting to the witness evidence this Court has heard previously from Prosecution witnesses as to times they met with Captain Radic at Nova Ulica 81 and nothing more than that. I'm certainly not trying to twist any of the words of Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Captain Radic went back to Nova Ulica 81 before 1.00 a.m. to go back to the house he'd been staying in and to go back to sleep in the bed he'd been sleeping in; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you put the question to me? I told you a moment ago this wasn't correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: This dinner, Mr. Zirojevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You made a good suggestion but I don't believe that my learned friend is proceeding along the correct road. This Prosecution witness who is being referred to never mentioned the dinner or when -- the period when they were leaving the dinner. I know what the case is. But the witness is in -- being misled to a statement that was never stated by anyone in this courtroom. The witness said: I met him at the dinner at 1.00. Now, you can put a statement to the witness and then ask him whether this is correct or not. As it is, it is misrepresentation of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I would submit I'm simply putting to the witness a contrary position based on Prosecution evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But is it based upon specific evidence or are you drawing inferences?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: A combination of the two, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's the drawing of inferences that's the problem, Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: It's -- the specific evidence refers to two witnesses, P-018 and P-022, who speak to returning to Nova Ulica 81 late in the evening of the 20th of November, 1991, between 10.00 a.m. to 1.00 a.m., and finding Captain Radic there -- sorry, 10.00 p.m., I beg your pardon. And they place Captain Radic at Nova Ulica 81 at those times. This is an alibi defence with regard to this aspect of the testimony, and I would submit that the Prosecution is entitled to put to this witness the inference that Captain Radic left early so that those witnesses that the Prosecution relies upon are indeed correct and are indeed telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can certainly, Mr. Lunny, put to the witness the Prosecution case that Captain Radic was not at the meeting after a certain time -- not at the dinner after a certain time if he was there at all, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But don't clothe it with the impression that it is the evidence of witnesses if it is, in fact, an inference you want to be drawn from the evidence of witnesses. You're just pushing it too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That was never my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Zirojevic, this dinner was also in Petrova Gora, and Nova Ulica was only a couple of minutes away by car; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dinner was at Petrova Gora but I wouldn't be able to agree with you that it was only a few minutes' drive by car.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: We've heard evidence at page 12.665 that Captain Radic had a car with him, isn't that true, at the dinner?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Zirojevic, isn't it true that Captain Radic left this meeting, left this dinner earlier than you're telling this Court, and he left well before 1.00 a.m.; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered in the negative. I said that it wasn't correct. We left the house together just before dawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You, Mr. Zirojevic, are stretching this dinner out to dawn to help your friend Captain Radic, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And after 15 years, you have no written record of this dinner whatsoever; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've put that question to me already, sir, and I told you that I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I could move on and move away from the dinner, Mr. Zirojevic. Yesterday you testified about changes in the make-up of Assault Detachment 1 in late October; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The change in the make-up of the assault detachment came about on several occasions. Among others, there was one change just before the fall of Vukovar, about a week before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: However, with regard to late October, you told us yesterday at page 48 that the changes brought the Leva Supoderica, the TO and the Petrova Gora into Assault Detachment 1. Do you remember saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late October, the TO Petrova Gora detachment and the TO Leva Supoderica detachment became part of the Assault Detachment 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And isn't it true, Mr. Zirojevic, that one of the reasons they were brought into Assault Detachment 1 was because of problems with cooperation between the various units fighting in Petrova Gora; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understand your question. What do you mean by "cooperation"? I'm not familiar with the term.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: As an officer of the JNA and as an officer of the Guards Brigade, you are not familiar with the term "cooperation"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Coordinated action, yes, I'm familiar with that. But as for cooperation, "kooperacija," that's not the term that I'm familiar with in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Before the TO and the Leva Supoderica and the Petrova Gora were brought into Assault Detachment 1, you were fighting in a coordinated fashion, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora TO detachments were in coordinated action with the Assault Detachment 1 in carrying out their combat missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And in carrying out those missions, there was cooperation between the various units involved, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is coordinated action between two units carrying out an attack along the same axis, in that the two units each have their own commands or commanders, depending on the unit involved. There has to be coordination; otherwise, there is confusion in the attack against the enemy. I coordinated my actions with the 3rd Motorised Company, as it did with me. So we had coordination in our -- in the execution of our combat missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And in the coordination between the Leva Supoderica, Petrova Gora and the 1st Assault Detachment before they were joined, there was confusion, wasn't there? That was the reason they fell together, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was confusion among the commanders of -- or, rather, between the commanders of the two TO detachments Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora and the motorised battalion. I don't know why the command of the Operations Group South decided that these two Territorial Defence units and the Motorised Battalion should fuse to form a new assault detachment for the purpose of the execution of the task. This is something that I was unable to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You testified yesterday about the assault detachment, but over and above that, rather, within that assault detachment, there were a number of assault groups, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of the battalion, or the commander of the assault detachment can form several assault groups with a view to carrying out specific tasks. It can set up at least one assault group or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And in the 1st Assault Detachment, there had been three companies and they became three assault groups; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A company cannot be an assault group. An assault group is a temporary establishment within combat disposition which is established in -- until a mission is completed and it can go up to the strength of a reinforced detachment, so that a company may not act as an assault group. A company may be an assault group but it has to be established by a higher command, a command higher than that of a battalion. A commander of a brigade may establish an assault group at the level of a company. But as I said, that's a higher level of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And Mr. Zirojevic, you, being the commander of the 2nd Motorised Company, you were placed in charge of a second assault group, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Within my company, an assault group was established, which was under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And under your command, there were also volunteers from Novi Sad, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Volunteers from Novi Sad were used for securing the lines that had been achieved. They did not take part in direct combat, no. They only secured part of -- or, rather, they only secured the front line and it was done by a part of the Novi Sad volunteer group.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: But that volunteer group was fighting along your axis, wasn't it, Mr. Zirojevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that they did not take part in direct combat, which is to say they were not part of offensive operations, no. They only secured the lines, the front line that had been reached. They were not professionally competent to take part in such operations as you described.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: But they secured the lines along your axis, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And they were subordinated to you for that purpose, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were attached to me; they were not subordinated to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I may have a moment, Mr. Zirojevic. You're the professional officer; these men were not professional, and whether they were attached or subordinated, they received orders from you, didn't they, Mr. Zirojevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the sense of security, the task aimed at securing. In that sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And this, Mr. Zirojevic, would be a good example of a single and unified chain of command, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand the question. What do you mean by a "unified chain of command"?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You couldn't have two commanders responsible for the same group of men at the same time, could you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally. The principle of singleness of command was applied in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And as your assault group was set up in that way on your axis, Captain Radic would have exercised command in the same way, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question because I don't know how he organised it in his axis, how it was organised along his axis. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You have just told us that singleness of command applied in the JNA. That applied along your axis and it also applied along the Captain Radic, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat once again: I don't know how Captain Radic organised these affairs along his axis. I don't know how he organised it. I told you that after combat operations were completed for the day, just before the night fell, I showed to the officers of volunteer units where to deploy these people. If you consider that to be a function of command, then, yes. But I don't think that that falls under the term "command," but that is your opinion, so be it. Which means that during daytime, they were not in direct combat, they were in the rear, resting, and only towards the rest of the day were they introduced in order to secure the lines reached, so that my people, members of the assault group, could rest during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Zirojevic, you have not answered the question that you were asked. You have told us a few minutes ago that singleness of command applied in the JNA. Now, I'm not asking you what you knew about what was happening from day to day. I'm asking you: That theory that applied to the JNA, as you have told us, would have applied also on Captain Radic's axis; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, once again, that I don't know what was applied along the axis of Captain Radic. I don't want to give you assumptions and tell you whether that was likely or not likely. I don't know that and I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: It was the doctrine and it was the rules that prevailed at the time. You had to follow it and Captain Radic had to follow it; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is that the rules were supposed to be delivered. Now whether that was the case, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You told us yesterday when you were talking about Captain Radic, you were asked by Mr. Borovic at the end of your evidence how good an officer he was. You were singing his praises. You also told us that the Guards Brigade were the elite. It's the case that that JNA doctrine was applied by Captain Radic, just as it was applied by you. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, you're putting the same question to me but in a different way. Can it be supposed, assumed? Yes. Now, whether that was indeed the case I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And it would need to be applied, Mr. Zirojevic, that singleness of command, because without it there would be confusion, wouldn't there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And without it, fighting in a built-up area, there would be accidents, wouldn't there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And that's why you applied it and that's why Captain Radic would have applied it; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're repeating the same question again. So I can only speculate and say yes. Now whether that was the case, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And as the Novi Sad volunteers were in your axis and received orders from you, the Leva Supoderica, the Petrova Gora, and the TO were in the axis of Captain Radic, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those units were neighbouring units to Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Zirojevic, we've heard evidence in this Court there were not neighbouring units but they were subordinated to Captain Radic underneath the 1st Assault Detachment. Captain Radic was in charge of the 3rd Assault Group and within that assault group there were the Leva Supoderica, the Petrova Gora and the TO; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I already spoke about that, saying that an assault group can be established at the level of the battalion up to the strength of a reinforced platoon. A detachment of TO in the establishment formation can be only equal to a battalion, so there cannot be a case where there are two TO detachment with an assault group which are both above or larger than a company within which an assault group of the strength of a reinforced platoon can be established. So theoretically, they could not have been part of an assault group established within the 3rd Motorised Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: The Leva Supoderica, Petrova Gora, and TO were fighting along the same axis as Captain Radic, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Petrova Gora TO detachment and the Leva Supoderica TO detachment were on the left side of the 1st Motorised Battalion. Since on the left frank of the 1st Motorised Brigade, there was the 3rd Motorised Company, automatically they were all neighbours of the 3rd Motorised Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: When you say "neighbours," how close are we talking about here, Mr. Zirojevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you about that because I don't have accurate information, but they could have been very close, which is to say, that if a part of the unit of Captain Radic, that is to say the 3rd Motorised Company, was moving along one side of a street, they could have been moving along the other side of the street. So they could have been just 10 metres apart, they could have been that close.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Captain Radic then, in your evidence, could have been fighting on the same -- the very same street as the Leva Supoderica and the Petrova Gora. You've told us about the need for singleness of command. You've told us that without it in a built-up area there would be a danger of accidents. If there was shooting and killing of your own forces by friendly fire, if we can call it that, by accident, there would be an inquiry, wouldn't there? The army would want to know what went wrong, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And for Petrova Gora, for 1991, there was no such inquiry because there were no such deaths by friendly fire, were there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. That wasn't within my competence. I simply don't know. Whether inquiry was made or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: After you left Vukovar, did you hear of any inquiry into any accidental deaths along Captain Radic's axis of attack?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And as the Novi Sad soldiers or volunteers took orders from you, the Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora, when fighting down the same street, took orders from Captain Radic, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely not. As an element of combat disposition within an assault detachment, they could have only received orders from the commander of assault detachment, not from a commander of the company of the 1st Motorised Battalion, if we are applying the principle of singleness of command. That is to say, the commander of the assault detachment is the commander to all units within that detachment and they can only receive orders from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I can move on, Mr. Zirojevic. You testified yesterday about meetings at the 1st Motorised Battalion headquarters and who attended those meetings; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that we had daily briefings at the command post of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And do you recall telling us that the Leva Supoderica TO and Petrova Gora leaders did not attend the same briefings as you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People who led the Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora units did not attend briefings at the 1st Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: As I understand it, yesterday in your evidence you also testified that on occasion, when you came out of the briefings, the leaders of the Leva Supoderica, Petrova Gora, and TO would be waiting there to go back -- rather, were waiting outside to go inside to receive their briefings. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Zirojevic, that with the giving of military orders, there is a need for clarity?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: There is a need for precision, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And there is a need for consistency, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would have to clarify the word "consistency" for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: For soldiers and their leaders fighting in the same area, you would not repeat an order twice and have two different briefings. You would issue the order to everyone at the one time to ensure that it was clear, that it was precise, and that everyone heard the same order, that it was consistent. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you, but in this particular case, commanders of various levels of units cannot all attend the same meeting. I told you already that detachment is a higher formation than a company. It was part of the assault group, so in addition to the 1st Motorised Battalion, there was the Leva Supoderica unit and the Petrova Gora unit. The fact of the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion was also simultaneously a commander of the detachment for a while is a different story. He would simply give out the tasks. He was first and foremost the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion and then he would go out and give tasks to others within the assault detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Moving on, Mr. Zirojevic, but again dealing with orders and communicating those orders. You testified yesterday about the use of Motorolas and the fact a single frequency was used for that. Do you recall giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And how many Motorolas did you have within the battalion at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that this was outside of the formation system, I think that there was 7 to 8, that is to say, that every company commander had his own Motorola, then the battalion commander had some, I think the commander had one and the deputy had another one. And that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And as I understand it, with this single frequency you described, only two people could communicate to each other at any given time; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that at one point in time, only two people could communicate. The others could listen on to their conversation but only two people could talk to each other, as is the case with any other radio equipment that is part of a network.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And that means, then, that if two company commanders were communicating, Major Tesic would not be able to communicate to the third company commander; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: In the case of an emergency, Major Tesic could not communicate with a third officer, could he?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to establish connection, one has to push an appropriate button on the Motorola. You have to say what you have and then release the button. The other person responding to you applies the same procedure. In the meantime, there are pauses between communication. Commander of the battalion was authorised to order silence on the frequency and then announce whatever he had to announce.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: How did you communicate, Mr. Zirojevic, with your subordinates?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lunny, is this a convenient time, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll have our first break now, and resume at 25 past because of redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Mr. Zirojevic, before the break, we were talking about communications and the use of the Motorola radios. You told us earlier today that your battalion had 7 or 8 in total for the entire battalion. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And you described who they were distributed to; Major Tesic, Stijakovic, the three company commanders. They would also be given to those in charge of mortar batteries, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the commander of the mortar battery and the commander of the anti-armour unit had them. And I believe I explained as much yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: So that's Mr. Tesic, Mr. Stijakovic, three commanders of the companies, that's five, mortar and artillery is 7. You said 7 or 8. That's all the Motorolas distributed, isn't it? They're all taken care of?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: How did you communicate with your own platoons within your company, Mr. Zirojevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the establishment means of communications and personally. One of the platoon commanders was killed at the very beginning on the 7th of October, one of my platoon commanders fell ill on the 10th of October and went back to Belgrade, and one platoon commander before we set out from Dubrava also fell ill, so that I spent most of the time alone with my soldiers. In view of the fact that the front line was not that wide, I was able to pass on my orders and communicate with my soldiers verbally, but I also used the radio communications device I had at my disposal, which was the RUP-33.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: We can move on now, Mr. Zirojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be obliged if we can move into private session for the next series of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in public session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: You and Mr. Vuckovic, you are staying in the same hotel, I take it, yes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: On what dates did you speak to the Defence about your evidence when you were here in The Hague this week, Mr. Zirojevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the day of my arrival and the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: If I may have one moment, please, Mr. Zirojevic. What times did you meet with the Defence on the Saturday and the Sunday, Mr. Zirojevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At around 12.00 and then at about 6.00 in the afternoon. That was the Saturday. On the Sunday, we met at 11.00 and were together until around 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one final question. I would be obliged if again we could move back into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: And did you speak to the Defence yesterday, Mr. Zirojevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zirojevic. I have no further questions for you. Obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zirojevic, do you know whether there appeared as witnesses before the ICTY Predrag Stefanovic, Captain Kopcic and Captain Bojkovski?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before leaving the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, what was your post in the army?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the commander of the 2nd Battalion -- of the 1st Battalion of the Guards Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be so kind as to tell me the following. Both my learned friend and I asked you about the Guards Motorised Brigade of where I your unit was part. Can you tell me the following: Which moral traits did the persons admitted into the Guards Motorised Brigade had to have?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: High moral integrity, no blemish in their personal background, and that of their fathers and grandfathers. For instance, when I became part of the Guards Motorised Brigade in Brcko, I learned from the senior officers who were involved in the selection more about the -- my family and the family of my wife than I, myself, knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they draw upon the personal backgrounds of your family, of your wife's family, and your grandfathers, and had they found a blemish in your background, could you have become a member of the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN ZIROJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not possible to be a member of the Guards Motorised Brigade if, among members of the most immediate family, there were persons who had a criminal record or had even been called to account for their political activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have completed my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zirojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Borovic. You will be pleased to know, sir, that that concludes the questioning in this trial of you. You are free to return to your ordinary activities. May we thank you for your attendance here and the assistance that you've given us. Thank you. And the court officer will show you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you please read allowed the affirmation on the card that is given to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, please tell the Trial Chamber your name, date and place of birth, your educational background, and your family status. Please, for interpretation's sake, take it slowly and carry on.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Davor Vuckovic. I was born on the 3rd of September -- on the 3rd of September, 1964, in Imotsko -- Imotski, the Republic of Croatia. I am married and have two sons. Before graduating from the military academy, I completed my primary education.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: In my home town of Imotski, whereupon I completed the military high school in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Vuckovic. Upon completing the military high school, you enrolled in the military academy. Where was that and what rank did you hold upon graduation?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I enrolled in the military academy in Belgrade in 1983 and I graduated in 1987 and was promoted to the rank of second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before leaving for the Vukovar front line, can you tell us which duties you held and in what -- with what rank?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Upon graduating from the military academy, I was assigned to the duty with the Guards Motorised Brigade, the 1st Motorised Battalion to the duty of platoon commander in a mortar battery.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Thereupon, in 1991, I became commander of that same battery.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: We will talk in greater detail about your activities in Vukovar later on. Please tell us: After the end of the Vukovar operations, which duties did you hold and which course did your military career take, and what is your occupation at present?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: In mid-1992, I was assigned to the duty of the battery commander in the 2nd Motorised Battalion and I stayed at that duty up until the end of 1994 when I was put to the duty of the commander of the 3rd Motorised Battalion, where I stayed until the month of May of 1998 when I was appointed deputy commander of the 2nd Guards Battalion, as it was called at the time, and I carried out that duty until the month of September of 2000 when I was appointed commander of the 2nd Guards Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuckovic, which rank did you hold when you held the duty of the commander of the 2nd Guards Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998, I was promoted to the rank of major and that was my rank at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And after that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: After that, I was assigned to the duty with the command of the Guards Brigade where I stayed until the month of November 2005. Thereupon, I was assigned to the duty of the chief of the department in the head of the -- or, rather, of the department in the office of the General Staff of the army of Serbia where I am at present.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The Guards Brigade was known to be an elite unit. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what sort of men of what moral traits and abilities could be admitted into the Guards Motorised Brigade? What sort of duties was the Guards Motorised Brigade assigned to in peacetime conditions?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Briefly, it could be put in the following way: I came to the Guards Brigade at the end of August 1997 [as interpreted]. However, already in the course of January 1997 -- or, rather, 1987, that was during my schooling, I was interviewed by superior officers as to whether I would wish to be assigned to the Guards Brigade. I received a definite answer about this only upon my graduation. Superior organs were basically checking me to see what my abilities were, what my family circumstances were, and my personal background was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned these checks or vetting. Can you tell us who it was who was unable to be admitted into the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No person with a criminal record could be admitted into the Guards Brigade. And not only the person contemplated to become a member of the Guards Brigade but also his or her family.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what the ethnic make-up of the Guards Motorised Brigade was and specifically in the battery whose commander you were before and during your time in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: The ethnic make-up was as follows: The -- all the peoples and minorities from the territory of the former Yugoslavia were represented in the Guards Motorised Brigade. I had soldiers from all republics and of all ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was the ethnic make-up the same at the point you were sent to Vukovar and did the same ethnic make-up of people eventually end up in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Soldiers of all ethnicities held all the different duties and specialties required.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you came to Vukovar, how many site-setters did you have in your -- or gunners did you have in your battery?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I had six artillery pieces or. Rather 120-millimetre mortars and I therefore had six gunners.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time in Vukovar, do you recall the ethnicities of these six gunners?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. By happenstance, there was the following ethnic make-up: There were three Croats, two Serbs, and as far as I remember, one Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The three Croat gunners, did they take direct part in the combat actions in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuckovic, can you tell the Trial Chamber what VES means and the procedure based upon which persons are sent to serve their military service or assigned to the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: VES is short for "military occupational specialty" and it consists of a code, of a four-digit code. For instance, I had scouts, signalmen, site-setters, gunners, soldiers manning the artillery pieces, and drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how the soldiers were being sent to their military service in terms of the territories where they would be sent and in terms of the needs for the reserve forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Every territorial organ, in accordance with its own needs or the needs of his Territorial Defence units or the units within their purview, planned and defined which VES would be of service and persons were sent for their military service accordingly. We, the unit carrying out the training, were unable to have any influence over the VES or to change it in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us when it was that you arrived with your battery at the Vukovar front line and what it was all like?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: We arrived there on the 1st of October. During the march along the way, we experienced some unpleasantries; namely, enemy fire in the sector in the village of Djeletovci and at the entrance to the village of Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Carry on, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: In Negoslavci, I was met by the chief of artillery of the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade, Lieutenant-Colonel Milorad Penic, who took me to the area where my fire position was. We took up positions, organised the positions, deployed the unit and prepared for action.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said a moment ago that there was enemy fire. Who was your enemy at the time of your arrival at the Vukovar front line and what were your tasks in such a situation where enemy fire was opened upon you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Croatian paramilitary forces. I consider them to be the enemy. Our task was to deblock the barracks in Vukovar, to liberate the civilian population that had been taken prisoner in town, or, to put it briefly, to establish law and order and freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Briefly, as the commander of the mortar battery, [microphone override] axis were you at the Vukovar theatre of war, were you tell us what axis of activity that was at the moment when you came to this assignment?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: By virtue of the fact that I was within the 1st Motorised Battalion, in terms of its establishment, it was only natural that I should be support to my battalion in combat activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know where the 3rd Motorised Company was and who commanded it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I know the 3rd Company was at Petrova Gora, Nova Ulica, and Sesta Proleterska neighbourhood. Captain Miroslav Radic was in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who was commanding the 2nd Company within the 1st Motorised Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The 2nd Company was commanded by Captain Zoran Zirojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever provide fire support along this axis and, if so, what did it look like, and along the axis of which company? Specifically which company?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My zone of activity was to the right in the street of Svetozara Markovica, to the left it was the railroad, and in depth, the Vuka River with -- focusing on the axis of activity of the 3rd Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say "focusing on the axis of activity of the 3rd Company," what does that mean specifically, and what does this "focus" mean in military terms, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: By virtue of my deployment along the axis of the 3rd Company, the commander of the 3rd Company of the battalion actually focused the activity on the 3rd Company, because the artillery officer who was providing support is always in the focus of the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you are on that axis of activity of the 3rd Company providing support, did you often see Captain Radic while he was engaged along this axis of his activity?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I did. I saw him every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And on that day, when there would be a lull in the fighting, would you see him after that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Because we spent many years together. We know each other; we were friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know where the observation post of Captain Radic was, where he was staying?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind as to tell the Court where this was?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: His observation post was in Nova Street. I think it was the fourth or fifth house on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Did you ever go to see Miroslav Radic at his observation post?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Several times?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us at the time when you went to the observation post, and of course that could not have been during the fire operations, but only after that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time, did you attend any kind of regular meeting or any kind of meeting, for that matter, that was held at the observation post of Captain Miroslav Radic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And did you ever hear of him having regular meetings with the commander of the TO Petrova Gora and the commander of Leva Supoderica?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever see meetings being held at that observation post that were attended by Colonel Mrksic in addition to Captain Radic, then Major Sljivancanin, Major Borivoje Tesic, and members of TO Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never saw Colonel Mrksic within the disposition of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And were you present on did you hear of some kind of regular meetings being held there of the persons that I just enumerated?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: This observation post that I'm asking you about, was it ever a command post for planning operations in terms of liberating Vukovar; at least that part of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I just know of two command posts and that is the command post of the 1st Motorised Battalion and the command post of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And did you ever hear of this house? Actually, a brief question before that. Do you know who owned this house where Captain Radic's observation post was?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell us.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this was the house of the father of Stanko Vujanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you say -- The interpreters are asking us to slow down because the names are not getting into the transcript but that will be dealt with. Do you know what Stanko Vujanovic looks like?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you came to visit Miroslav Radic at the observation post, now my specific question is as follows: Did you see him there every day, and did he go to the observation post at all?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I never saw him in that house and I never saw him in front of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And at the observation post, were you ever present or did you hear of Radic having meetings with the commander of the TO Petrova Gora and the commander of Leva Supoderica, and do you know what these people's names were? And then to put it the other way around, did you ever hear or see --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the question.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not hear or see these people but I know these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What are their names?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the TO at first was Jaksic and then Miroljub Vujovic. As for Leva Supoderica, there was a man named Kameni.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I put another question to you that is not in the transcript. I will repeat it. Were you ever present or did you hear that Captain Miroslav Radic with Miroljub Vujovic and Lancuzanin, nicknamed Kameni, that he had meetings with them in terms of planning operations in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I never heard that have and I never saw anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. When you came to the observation post of Miroslav Radic, did you ever see any kind of detention centre there or prison, did you ever see any prisoners there where Miroslav Radic's observation post was?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vuckovic, could you briefly tell us how these units of the Territorial Defence functioned and whether they cooperated, acted in concert with the 1st Motorised Battalion or, more specifically, how did they function? You tell us whether there was cooperation or not.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
