utterances.text: As far as I can remember, units of the TO always acted in concert with the 1st Motorised Battalion in carrying out combat activities in the following way: The battalion commander would issue orders or, rather, tasks to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the role of the battalion was in establishing JOD 1 or, rather, where was it in terms of JOD 1 and the 1st Motorised Battalion, and do you know anything about the existence of assault groups?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: By virtue of the fact that Major Borivoje Tesic was the most senior-ranking officer there and the best trained, educated officer in that area, he was appointed commander of the 1st Assault Detachment. His task was to command and issue tasks to all units that were within Assault Detachment 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to lead so I'm going to ask you: Where was the command post of Major Tesic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: The command post of Major Tesic was in the street of Svetozara Markovica. When viewed from Negoslavci, it's after the railroad. I think the seventh or eighth house on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was at that command post and were there any regular briefings there by you company commanders?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: At the command post, in addition to Major Tesic, Captain First Class Slavko Stijakovic was there as his deputy. Then a reserve captain whose name I do not recall. Then Staff Sergeant Bojic and Sergeant Stamenkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any regular briefings at the command post, and who came to these regular briefings, if any?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Briefings took place every day regardless of whether there was activity or whether there was a cease-fire. All company commanders came to the briefing and I, as the commander of the battery.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what time was this usually this command post, this briefing, and is that where you were given your assignments and tasks for the following day?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: The briefings usually took place sometime between 1900 hours up to 2100 hours, actually. At these briefings, there would be an analysis of the activities that took place on that day and we were given assignments for the following day, for the activity that was to take place on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At these regular briefings when you were given tasks for the following day, was Miroljub Vujovic, the commander of the Petrova Gora territorial detachment, ever present?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: This was the briefing of the 1st Motorised Battalion and by virtue of that fact Mr. Vujovic did not attend these briefings

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did it ever happen that the commander of the Leva Supoderica Detachment, Lancuzanin, was ever present at a regular briefing?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever see them at any point in time at the command post of the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion and at the same time the commander of the 1st JOD?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw them but only when we would finish our briefing, and as we would leave I would see them in the yard in front of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever hear of them getting assignments there from Commander Tesic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not hear of that because I was not present but that was probably the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, in relation to this command post, did anyone provide security there and, if so, who was it that secured it; and what was the regimen of access to that command post, meaning could a regular soldier, an ordinary soldier your enter the premises where the briefing was taking police station or could anyone get nearby?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: At the very outset of the combat activity, that is to say at the beginning of October until I became familiar with the terrain, or rather until I became familiar with what the safe and what the unsafe areas were, I had one or two soldiers accompanying me from my unit, and upon arrival at the command post, they could never enter the yard, let alone the house. We would put them up in the house across the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I did not fully follow this. Did you tell us who it was that provided security there? What was the composition of the security detail of the command post of the 1st Motorised Battalion, the 1st JOD?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Security of the command post was carried out by the platoon of the military police from the 2nd Battalion of the military police. That was assigned to the battalion with that purpose in mind. At the entrance into the yard of the command post, there were always two soldiers who were military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. As for your artillery support tasks that we've already referred to, you carry them out in accordance with whose plan and on whose exclusive orders?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: In the evening, during the briefing, the battalion commander would give me precise tasks in terms of who I was to support on the following day, in what area and possibly additional tasks related to something else. That is what I wish to say. Because it would happen that during the course of the day, the commander would ask me to come to the command post to issue other tasks to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did the commander do that during the day, Commander Borivoje Tesic, how would he communicate?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: He would call me by a means of communication, that is to say, the Motorola that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have your own couriers and when were these Motorolas introduced as a means of communication within the 1st Motorised Battalion? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Within the artillery units, there are no couriers for the simple reason that the artillery communication system is a much more complex one and a multi-level one in comparison with infantry units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So what means of communication do you use in the artillery in addition to the Motorola you used to communicate with Major Tesic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of combat operations, in order to establish contact with my unit, I mostly used wire communication, that is to say field telephones. Whenever that line was down, for whatever reason, the other means of communication was the radio relay, and then as the ultimate solution we would use radio communication. I'm now referring to the communication between myself and my unit which was at the firing position. As for communication between myself and other company commanders and the battalion command, the main means of communication there is the radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that in a mortar battery there are no couriers. Did you personally have a security detail or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: As I have said previously, I had that only during the first four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you came to the command post in November of 1991, did you come there on your own or were there people escorting you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I came entirely on my own, and mostly I would come in a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about other company commanders when they came to the command post for regular briefings. Did they bring along couriers or their security officers or would they also come by themselves as you did?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: They would always come on their own because there was no need for any security detail whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You and other company commanders, did you have an observation post where you spent time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: It was in Oslobodjenje Street in Petrova Gora settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During these combat operations, that is to say as you were providing firing support, did you ever change the location of your observation post and did that depend on some factors, or would some factors prompt that, or did it have anything to do with the specific task that you were given?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: My position in relation to other commanders was quite unique for the simple fact that I moved about and always created new observation posts in order to have better visibility and better ability to observe the deployment of our forces and to be able to see the objectives better.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please tell the Chamber, before the fall of Vukovar, in which location was your last observation post located?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: My last observation post which I took sometime around the 7th of November was in the sector of the school called 2nd Congress.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And this sector of the school 2nd Congress -- actually, that's the name of the school, right? It was called the 2nd Congress school?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe in closer terms where this sector is topographically?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes this school is located between the Sesta Proleterska settlement and Bosko Buha settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From that location, from that observation post were you able to see the bridges on the Vuka River, did you have visual control over that area?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have visual control of the area in the hospital sector from that observation post?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that's far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We spoke about the system of communication within the artillery independent of the communication system that existed within the battalion. Can you tell us whether that system was centralised, and what does it mean when, for example, a cease-fire is announced, or a truce, what kind of problems could arise? And for the purposes of your tasks, how could you communicate? How could you establish communication at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I, as an artillery officer, and somebody who was in charge of observation monitoring was informed by two sides about any cease-fire. I would be informed by the commander of the battalion, and I would also be informed by my superior artillery officers. As soon as a cease-fire was announced, or a truce, our lines were disconnected. Our lines of communication with the units deployed at firing positions so that we couldn't give an order for them to fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you spoke about the direction of activities of the 3rd Company and as you were giving fire support, were you able to see who was present in that direction of activity?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: As I have already told you, I changed my observation post depending on the activities I had for that day, and depending on my tasks. From my observation post, I would always see and survey the movements of our units, that is to say, the units of the 3rd Motorised Company and the TO units, and I would also survey and observe firing points or targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since this is something that my learned friends from the OTP are extremely interested in, tell me, if we have that direction of operation, who else acted in coordination with the 3rd Company?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence under the command of Miroljub Vujovic and Leva Supoderica detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: From your observation post when following activities in that axis, activities of the 3rd Motorised Company, were you able to see who issued orders to the members of the Leva Supoderica unit and who issued orders to the members of 3rd Company?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, mostly I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Judges?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: In order to protect the young soldiers, there would always be members of TO moving ahead of young soldiers because they were more familiar with the terrain; they had more combat experience and they were older. They were always commanded by Miroljub Vujovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about Captain Radic. Just a minute please. Captain Radic, in the direction of the activity when you were following the entire operation, to put it in layman's terms, were you able to see to whom he issued orders and what did these persons who received orders from him do?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Captain Radic always commanded his soldiers from his company and they were always behind the TO people, moving and taking the points that had been cleared and liberated by the TO members.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vuckovic, do you know -- or, rather, have you ever heard of Milovo Brdo or Milovo hill and do you know where it is?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: It is to the east of Bosko Buha settlement, that is to say between the Bosko Buha settlement and the bridges, or as we used to call that area, log market or timber market.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know on which date Milovo Brdo was taken or captured?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. That was on the 10th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that? And could you please explain to the Chamber how come you remember precisely that date?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that date because there was great joy among all of us. We were all excited because we knew that that was the last task in our area and that by liberating Milovo Brdo, we had accomplished the mission that we received from our superior command and our excitement was even greater because we were the only unit within the operations group that had managed to accomplish its mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say "units," do you mean the 1st Motorised Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Now, after you accomplished that mission, that particular mission and until the fall of Vukovar, what specific task did you have from the 10th or 11th -- or, rather, from the 10th of November, 1991, until the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: My task was to control or survey the area in front of the lines reached in the direction of the Vuka River, and to the left, towards the Luzac settlement, because from my observation point, I had a very good visibility over that area. The purpose of this was to avert incursion of any forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you say "I had good visibility," "I had visual control," what does that mean? What would you do if there was an emergency and under whose orders?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Had I observed that there was a movement of some units of paramilitary forces, my task was to inform the battalion command of it and they, in turn, would inform the command of the operations group because our area was inclusive of the Vuka River. Then, most likely, somebody would have taken some measures or opened fire against those targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know on which date Vukovar was liberated?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Since it seems to be an important date, or at least it was within your combat tasks, would you please tell us what date it was?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly. On the 18th, in the afternoon hours, we were informed that the negotiations with the paramilitary forces of Croatia were in progress and that they were about to surrender, most likely, and we consider that moment to be the end of hostilities and the moment of their surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you eventually hear that the paramilitary formations surrendered on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that. It was communicated to me from the communications centre of artillery by my artillery commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Penic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we are approaching our break, would you please tell me: In relation to your battery from the 10th of November, 1991, until the liberation of Vukovar, what positions did you occupy throughout that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I was mostly on my observation point next to the 2nd Congress school.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is this specifically the broader sector of Milovo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear -- did you see at that time in the broader sector of Milovo Brdo whether there were any units of the 1st Motorised Battalion there and, if so, which ones?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that on the 10th of November, when Milovo Brdo was liberated, in that axis, I supported and the 3rd Motorised Company was active in that axis as far as the battalion is concerned. That is to say, all forces that were along the axis Nova street, Sesta Proleterska settlement was completely the same as in the operation of liberating Milovo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's fine. That was until it was liberated. And when Milovo Brdo was liberated, what tasks were given to the units in that sector? Did they remain in Milovo Brdo sector or did they move forward, elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you previously. When we had briefing with our battalion commander, as I have already said, we received specific, precise tasks. Sometimes towards the 12th, if I remember well, at the briefing, the battalion commander issued an order to the companies to reinforce the lines reached and to remain in that area. And as for other forces from the assault detachment, they were to continue activities outside of our area, if I can put it that way. I didn't inquire further about it because that was outside of my area and I did not provide support to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to protect the lines reached, to preserve them, in addition to members of the 3rd and 4th Company, did you hear, did you see, did you observe alongside with them members of the Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica units?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see them and I wasn't interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did they and JOD 1 have a different area of activity?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this would be a convenient time for our break because I'm about to move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. We will resume at 2.00 p.m. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuckovic, you mentioned Motorolas. Do you know how many Motorolas there were in the 1st Motorised Battalion and how the work with Motorolas functioned?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know -- as far as I know, there were about 8 Motorolas in the battalion. The company commanders had them. I had one. The officers from the battalion command had them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us in practical terms how this functioned on the ground?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It functioned as follows: They were all on the same channel which changed from time to time. And all persons, or rather, all officers who had Motorolas were on the same channel and heard all the conversations taking place on that channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that if you were on this channel and Major Tesic was issuing an order to another company commander that you could hear at the same time the content and text of that order?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you defined the 18th of November as the date when Vukovar was liberated. The question is the following -- or, rather, you told us even how you were informed of the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So in terms of fire support, did you have any fire support at all on that day? You told us about the previous days but now we're talking about the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, I did not have any firing activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And were you on the same position where you were during the previous days?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that if a company would have had a task that you could have offered fire support from the position where you were?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: To the companies, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the following day, on the 19th of November, did you move anywhere from the area of Milovo Brdo? Specifically, where were you yourself on the 19th of November, 1991; that is to say, a day after the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: On orders from the commander of the battalion, Major Tesic, there was issued to me on the evening of the 18th during the briefing my task was to be at the observation post and to be on the ready for possible activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 19th in the morning, on that day, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: On the morning of the 19th, like almost every other day, sometime around 7.00, I came to the observation post, I placed the equipment there, and I prepared for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any Motorola communication on that day with anyone, Commander Tesic, Major Tesic or someone from the companies that were within the 1st Motorised Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: My Motorola was on -- or, rather, it was working in the system and since there was no need to engage in action, I was not in direct communication, if I can put it that way, but I was on the channel that was valid for that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that day, since you say that you were on that channel, your Motorola was, did you hear Major Tesic issuing an order to anyone on that day, and if so, tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that he first issued a task to Major Zirojevic and then to Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear the task for Captain Zirojevic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: The task for Captain Zirojevic was that he should go to the Dunav hotel, the Danube hotel, and that he should inspect the hotel. To clean it up - that was the jargon that was used in those days - and to provide security.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear what kind of order he issued to Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard. Major Tesic issued an order to Captain Radic that with part of his soldiers he should set out towards the area of the hospital and to place external security of the hospital there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that what the order was?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of order if he did issue an order to Captain Bojkovski, he issued to him, that is to say, the commander of the 1st Company?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Captain Bojkovski got his order on the previous evening during the briefing that he should reinforce his positions and remain in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that, since that was in the morning, I asked you about that, do you know when they went to carry out this task and whether they went out to carry out this task?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Like all other tasks, they went to finish this task immediately. They got their people and they went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether you had a regular briefing on the evening of the 19th of November, 1991, and who was present?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: On the evening of the 19th, we had the classical regular briefing that was attended by officers, like on all other days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the next day, the 20th of November, you and your battery, did you have any tasks?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of November, in the morning, I was given a task to change the direction of my artillery pieces, that is to say, the direction to the village of Bogdanovci in order to repel a possible attack at our positions from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how is direction changed? Could you explain that to us a bit, what does that mean? In what axis of activity do you possibly provide fire support in such a case?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Changing the direction of an artillery unit in terms of a new direction of activity calls for certain fortifications, or to put it in simpler terms, to do certain things with the soil there and then certain mathematical operations. At any rate, it's a process that goes on for a few hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you answered a few moments ago that you heard of the orders to the company commanders, my question now is: Were you next to them when they were receiving those orders or did you just hear this through the Motorola? Were you at another place then? Were you right by them or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I was at my own observation post next to the school of the 2nd Congress, Drugi Kongres, that is to say that I was not next to them but I was within the communication system.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From the place that was then your observation point, could you see the timber market? Do you know where it was?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I know where it is, but I did not have full visibility, only partial visibility, just a small part.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: It is below Milovo Brdo in the area before the bridges across the Vuka River.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 20th of November in the evening, did a regular briefing again take place and, if so, who was present there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat once again: A briefing was held every evening. That is to say that every evening, these briefings were attended by the same officers. On the 20th, again, it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about the evening of the 20th. Was Major Tesic present?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I wanted to explain. At the beginning of the briefing, they were all there. Major Tesic, after about half an hour, went to the command of the operations group.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who continued chairing the meeting that was this briefing actually?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: His deputy, according to establishment, Captain Stijakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember that second evening after the fall of Vukovar where it was that you went after that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: After the briefing was over, I went to my own area, or my own observation post, if I can call it that way, where I was awaited by the soldiers and some of the neighbours from the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the other company commanders went? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I know because after the briefing was over, I invited all of those present to come when they could to my place, because my neighbours insisted that they prepare some dinner and that we sort of socialise there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So who was present, in addition to the people from your unit and the neighbours from among the members of the 1st Motorised Battalion at that dinner?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Regrettably, most of them could not come but Captain Zirojevic came, Captain Radic came.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us a bit more about this dinner which is important for us here, not as a dinner, but as a moment which is mentioned during those days between the 18th and 24th of November. Can you tell us a bit more about it, what you did there, how long did you stay, what you talked about? If you can remember all of that and what it looked like, generally speaking, because you are our main witness with regard to this event.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the way it was: Since my observation post, in relation to all the others, was at the safest place of all, or rather in a street where there was no combat activity, in a street where people, if I can put it that way, lived normal lives to the extent that it was possible then. Not a single house was empty. How should I put this? Not a single house was badly damaged. I have a -- I had a very close relationship with the population there, and as a token of their gratitude, they wished -- or, rather, they asked me whether they could organise or prepare some food and that I should organise a dinner that would be attended by officers from the battalion. Of course I accepted. We helped with certain supplies that we had and that we provided and they, among the other small things there, they roasted a pig. Things like that. They made a particular effort for this to be - how should I put this - in a family environment so that the atmosphere would be very pleasant starting from the way the food was prepared, served, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this the first dinner of this kind that you had after you came to Vukovar until the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the first dinner in that composition and in that environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how long Captain Radic stayed at that dinner and how long you were there before you went to sleep?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know for a simple reason because it was almost daybreak. And as far as all our activities on the following day were concerned, we practically had to resort to the last atoms of our energy left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was stated here that Captain Radic went sometime after 1.00 at night, after midnight, or do you stand by what you said, that you left in the morning?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I stand by what I said. It's quite simply impossible for him to have left earlier because practically everyone left together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember in what part of the house you were seated and what the seating order was, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I do. In the front part of the house, or rather in the part of the house facing the Oslobodjenje Street, there was a large room which was in fact a dining-room together with the kitchen, as it were. I stayed in that house for a month and a half, and I know very well what the layout of the rooms was like. Tables were put together and chairs were around them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where you were seated in relation to Captains Radic and Zirojevic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Since the three of us were the only active-duty officers there, Radic sat at the head of the table, Zirojevic and I sat next to him. And we remained thus seated throughout the evening. We were close to the corner, to the left-hand side and there was no need for us to get up because nobody was passing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the evening of the 20th of November when you attended the dinner, did you know what your task was going to be on the following day, the 21st of November?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: We received our task from Deputy Commander Captain Stijakovic and it had to do with the inspection that he, as an officer, several months earlier he had come from the school, wanted to organise in order for the guards unit to maintain its high level and to inspect the troops to see whether they were all in proper order, clean, their hairs properly cut and their faces clean-shaven.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the 21st of November, the day after the dinner, was the inspection of the units in the first garrison of the battalion, in fact, carried out?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes it was. My unit's turn came at around noon. Captain Stijakovic came to the firing position which was about 3 kilometres away from us in the direction of Negoslavci and carried out the inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you talk to Major Tesic about the dinner and about the fact that you had stayed there for quite a while with Captain Radic, did you tell him this?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I told him because I had been criticised by Captain Stijakovic with regard to the state of matters in the unit and because the entire day on the 21st of November, I spent trying to redress these deficiencies. In the evening, as Major Tesic returned from Belgrade, he noticed that I was angry and tired and as I was on closer terms with him because he was the platoon commander of mine at the academy, he wanted to talk to me about this. It was at that point that I explained everything to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: About the dinner?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell him that Radic was there with you that night?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the evening of the 21st, do you remember where you were following the briefing and the discussion you had with Major Tesic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 21st, after the end of the briefing, Captain Zirojevic asked me to come to his observation post which I, to be quite frank, tried to refuse. However, on his insistence, I went there and spent about half an hour there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Radic there as well?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vuckovic, since you were oftentimes at the observation post, you were along the same axis, you were in Vukovar, what can you tell about Miroslav Radic's character, personal traits, about him as a soldier, his military abilities, moral qualities, and all the other characteristics that speak of his moral -- of him as a moral and military person?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Radic is the exemplary soldier and he proved as much in his work both before Vukovar and after. He was the exemplary soldier of the Guards Brigade, and he was a responsible person, extremely honest, a family man with -- without any vice and, to put it in short, a top-notch professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vuckovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have completed my examination of the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic. Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuckovic, I am one of the lawyers for Mr. Sljivancanin, and I will put several questions to you that are of interest to his Defence team. Tell us, do you know Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: At the time of your stay in Vukovar, did you have any contacts with him?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain the -- to the Trial Chamber and to us the purpose of these contacts, where they took place and what the substance of them was?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of combat activities, Major Sljivancanin would come to my observation point oftentimes, or rather to my observation points because I -- I changed them. He inquired after the situation in the unit, the objectives we had, or rather the targets that we were able to detect, the forces that I was able to gauge from the observation post and in general about the activities of artillery and whether there were any problems there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did Major Sljivancanin ever issue an order to you or try to issue an order to you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke of the information that was of interest to Major Sljivancanin which concerned artillery, enemy forces, the positions and so on and so forth. Can you explain to us what sort of artillery pieces the paramilitary formations of the Croatian army used, of the so-called Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can, for the simple reason that I am a professional and on the basis of the debris left by the artillery projectiles fired by the Croatian forces and the directions to which these -- the debris scattered I was able to infer the type of activity, the calibre, these were mortars, 60 millimetre, 82 millimetre. I was also able to establish that we were fired upon by these so-called partisan, one-barreled rocket launcher of the calibre 128-millimetres. We were also shot at by the 152-millimetre Howitzer for which I established that it fired from the direction of Nustar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the information you thus gathered, were you able to detect any other positions of the artillery of the so-called Croatian army in addition to Nustar?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: The position of their weapons was very difficult to uncover for the reason that they constantly moved their weapons and changed position. At the end of the combat activities, we found several mortars mounted on trailers of some sort of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Vuckovic, let me ask you this: Were there problems in artillery fire by the JNA in terms of lack of precision, and if so, could this affect the security of units as such?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were problems on several occasions. These problems boiled down to the fact that certain weapons fired projectiles that fell short of targets. In the interest of security, the officers had to establish what was going on and why. I learned later that these were technical problems, they were not deliberate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, I can conclude that in contacts with the security officer, with Major Sljivancanin, if there were such problems, you also informed him thereof because it was of interest to the security of the unit?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, because this was a huge problem which could cause friction among men and it had to be solved as a matter of urgency.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vuckovic, I think we met before in Belgrade, if you recognise me with my robes still on. Can we just deal with one or two matters that occurred in Belgrade when I saw you. It's right to say that you consider that you owe your life to Mr. Radic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's right to say that you actually believe that you owe him your life on no less than two occasions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is also correct that he owes me his life on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think it's also right to say that unfortunately you had a brother who was killed in the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when I was speaking to you briefly at Belgrade, I think you indicated that you considered Radic as being almost like a brother to you now; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The conversation wasn't that brief; it lasted an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I think it lasted 30 --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: An hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have got the timings, if you wish. Time sometimes move much quicker and slower than you imagine as this trial, I'm sure, will be able to understand in stress situations [sic]. But it's right, I think, you view Mr. Radic as akin to a brother. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you also described Mr. Radic as the sort of person who would take a blow to protect others, even though he may not have been involved in that particular act. That's correct also, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be allowed to explain what I meant by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Before we go, go any further, you accept you said that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you have to explain Bench, I'm sure they will want to hear.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that Captain Radic, just as any other professional officer of discipline and responsibility of the JNA who completed all the schools he did, is ready to take upon himself full responsibility for all the matters that take place in his area of responsibility and within his unit. That was what I meant when I stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Of course, we would say that Mr. Mrksic perhaps does not adhere to that particular view. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I stated my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's also right to say that you said that you wanted to find out the truth but you wanted to help your friend Mr. Radic so he could be released. That is correct also, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal with one or two other matters? Clearly you've given evidence for a period of time, but if I try and summarise it, could I suggest, perhaps, it comes down to five principal heads. The first head would be your evidence that the TO Vukovar Leva Supoderica were not subordinated at any time to the guards battalion and the 3rd Company when we're talking about Mr. Radic. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were in coordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: At no time were they ever subordinated, that's what you're actually saying. That is the guts of your evidence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Secondly, that the battalion stopped its military -- significant military activities on the 10th of November. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if -- I'm not trying to trivialise it in any way, the guards soldiers were protecting houses up in the heights rather like a Serbian securitas; isn't that right? They weren't fighting.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the guards soldiers, that is to say, the soldiers who were not wounded, who were not ill, performed that because in every company, there were between 30 and 40 soldiers remaining and, simply speaking, that is not a sufficient force that can continue to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So I take it that the answer to my question is that the fighting stopped for the guards battalion on the 10th of November. For whatever reason, it stopped. That's what you're saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the third point which you seem to be giving evidence on is that -- again, not trying to trivialise it, that of all the orders in all the world that you heard, you happened to hear Major Tesic issuing an order over the telephone to Radic on the 19th of November to go to the hospital. You've given evidence about that; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me correct you. Not telephone line but, rather, radio communication. And yes, I heard. I heard that order for that date. Otherwise, we were on line incessantly, 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. But you remember that quite clearly. That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: 15 years after the event you remember that order?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Fourthly, that you had a dinner of which Mr. Radic attended, along with others, on the evening of the 20th and that he stayed to daybreak. That's also one of your principal parts of evidence; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that you told Major Tesic on the 21st: By the way, I had dinner with Radic on the night of the 20th. That's correct, that's what your evidence is?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Tesic asked me why I looked the way I looked at that time and then I explained to him the reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then fifthly, that he is an exemplary officer. Now, there are other topics which I will deal with, but I want to deal with really the following question: Reflection of time, passage of time, would you describe the then Major Tesic as an excellent officer?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He is an officer who taught me what discipline was, as well as responsibility, honesty, professionalism, and who hated alcohol above anything else. This is why, on the 21st, I talked to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say -- I think he was your commander at the college; is that right? He was your platoon commander when you were at the military college; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think he's risen to great heights, has he not? What rank did he achieve?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he advanced in his career, and now he is a general within the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if one was to use one word to sum up Tesic, if I may use the surname in that way, would the word "integrity" be the appropriate word?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I consider him to be an outstanding professional and a disciplined officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's right to say that Major Tesic, as we know him, is a person who is easily contactable. Obviously one has to go through channels, but he is not a man who is a hermit hiding in a cave.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't consider at all that he was a man who would be hiding. I continue to have a lot of respect for him to this day, and I don't think that I said anything that could offend him or hurt him in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you remember I said the first plank was in relation to your evidence that you are saying, and others have said, that the TO were not subordinated to the 1st Battalion or, in this case, the 3rd Company? Would it surprise you if I told you that Major Tesic, in his statements, both to the Office of the Prosecutor and to Belgrade indicated, and I read: "The 3rd Assault Group conducted by Milorad Radic also comprised a TO Vukovar detachment led by Vojnovic which comprised the TO Petrova Gora as well as the Leva Supoderica." Would that surprise you that he has said that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: It would surprise me because that is not consistent with what transpired on the ground. Initially, the TO acted in coordination with the battalion, and later on it acted in coordination with the 3rd Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But the situation is you are an officer from the guards battalion, if I may use that, and you have given very clear evidence, well aware of the consequences of your evidence and the importance of this issue. Now, someone is wrong. Either you're wrong, or the commander of the battalion is wrong because there is no middle ground, is there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I gave an oath here. This is what we call in Serbia an oath, and I also gave an oath to my country and to my army. I'm still an active officer, and I consider myself to be an honourable and decent person. I think that I've answered sufficiently to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not suggesting that you're lying. I am simply suggesting to you that here is the commander of the battalion where singleness of command is essential, and he is saying in two instances, Belgrade and OTP statement, that in actual fact Mr. Radic's unit comprised of TO Vukovar, which also surprised of TO Petrova Gora, as well as the Leva Supoderica numbering between 30 and 40 men whose commander was Milan Lancuzanin, a la Kameni. So might it be that he is right being the commander of the battalion and you are wrong?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No, for the simple reason that I spent 40 days in that axis, day after day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, then can you just give, not only myself but perhaps this Bench and other people listening, how it is that the commander of battalion has been working on the basis that the TO are actually subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot explain that. I just know the facts which took place and I know what I saw on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Explain to us, please, what "singleness of command" means?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Singleness of command means, for example, specifically in a battalion, nobody but the battalion commander can command the battalion, and that I, as a battery commander, cannot receive orders from anyone else but him or that my deputy cannot receive orders from anyone else but me. In other words, if somebody else attempts to issue an order to him, somebody who is senior in rank, then my deputy needs to inform me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's take a hypothetical situation on the evidence that you have given. We have the TO, you say they are not subordinated to Tesic. You say they are subordinated to whom, Jaksic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, then, how does one have singleness of command when you have Tesic saying, quite simply, that this particular unit or units were attached to Radic's company, and therefore would be subsumed within the command structure of that company?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Jaksic commanded the Territorial Defence. Now as to whether he received any tasks from Tesic, whether something transpired there, I don't know, because I didn't attend those meetings. During the execution of combat operations, I stayed in communication, and I coordinated the work only of company commanders within the composition of the 1st Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But if what you say is correct, then there would be no need for people like Lancuzanin and Vujanovic to go to Tesic's headquarters for briefing because they are not subordinated to him. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I only know about the structure and subordination within the 1st Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could you answer my questions, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that they were subordinated to the battalion and battalion commander or to the command of the assault detachment, let's clarify that first. Because I believe from my point of view that Major Tesic had two roles. He was both the battalion commander and commander of the assault detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But Major Tesic says, quite simply, that the TO was subordinated to him and Captain Radic. You say: No, no, that's certainly not the case, there is another almost parallel command structure. And I'm saying if that is the case, you would not, therefore, expect to see people like Lancuzanin and Vujovic at Tesic's headquarters with regular officers because it's the wrong line of command for subordination. Can Mr. Borovic please keep his voice down.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: One thing. You say "parallel." It was not parallel. Tesic, as commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion, conducted briefings with company commanders and myself as a battery commander at the command post of the battalion and that -- he also issued tasks to us. Later on, later on, commanders of the TO would come to him because I used to see them in the yard as well as commanders of Leva Supoderica. And at that time, he, as commander of the assault detachment based on the tasks he had already issued to us, would issue tasks to him -- to them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If what you say is right, can you explain then the following: "Vujanovic and Lancuzanin came occasionally until the fall of Vukovar but Vujovic and Captain Radic came regularly. I would be lying if I said that the relationship between Captain Radic and Kameni or Vujovic was not friendly. I know that Radic's orders were fully complied with." Can you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what Major Tesic stated. All I know and all I'm telling you is what I saw and the impression that I had. It wasn't my impression that there was closeness in their relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's move on to another topic. Would you agree with the fact that -- or the following statement: "TO Vukovar were not forces that one could rely on." It's from, by the way, Major Tesic, in fairness to everybody. Do you agree with that? "TO Vukovar were not forces that one could rely on." To help you a little bit further: "Sometimes we had to delay operations either because TO Vukovar did not show up or if they did show up, they did not feel like fighting."

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: The operations were delayed, that's true, but it's also true that their combat experience was much greater than ours. They were also much more familiar with the terrain and it is also true that they wanted to liberate their town. So this statement that they could not be relied on is simply, in my view, not a true one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me that my learned friend is to certain extent abusing the rights given to him by the Chamber. I don't see any reason for him to be reading page by page a statement that a witness gave to the OTP and to put that to the witness who keeps denying that that's true. I think that an individual statement could be put to the witness in a different context, but to take the entire statement and read it in its entirety, that's wrong. Why don't they bring witness Tesic here and if they were to bring witness Tesic here and we cross-examine -- and if we were to cross-examine him, then we would see whether anything would remain standing, anything contained in that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you agree with that analysis of TO Vukovar or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No, and I gave you my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with the 10th of November. You said that basically the battalion -- others have said so you're not misled. Others have said that the battalion stopped on the 10th of November, and you have said today: Well, there were only 30 or 40 men -- standing men left; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I never mentioned reserve forces. I said that in companies there remained 30 to 40 regular soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I didn't -- I wasn't aware I had mentioned reserve forces; if I have, I apologise. I don't see it. But let's deal with it this way. I think that you say there remained 30 to 40 regular soldiers, my words, who were fit to fight. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No, one couldn't say so. Because if there remained 30 to 40 soldiers in a company, times three companies, which is what we had, this adds up to 120 soldiers. I'm referring to infantry people who were in direct combat. That did not include the military police platoon, that did not include my battery, the logistics platoon, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I didn't say 30 or 40 people in the company. I mentioned 30 to 40 regular soldiers who were fit to fight. So I want to know how many soldiers were fit to fight, in toto?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I told you, in three companies, 30 to 40 soldiers in each, that adds up to 120 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So it adds up basically to a company, fully staffed company, doesn't it? A company is normally about 90?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These three infantry companies came to Vukovar with about 90 soldiers each.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So what was it that these battle-hardened soldiers were then doing after the 10th?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: These soldiers were positioned in the lines reached. They reinforced the reached lines and they conducted what we soldiers call firing control of the area in front of them. And occasionally, they would try to move the line a bit but not to a significant extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So what you are saying is that the elite guards battalion, and I wasn't using "battle-hardened" in a pejorative way, because they had been through a difficult time, these soldiers were basically left to look after houses by way of consolidation? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the simple reason to attempt to prevent anyone else from getting killed, wounded or hurt. We tried to preserve our men, these young soldiers who happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if there was any suggestion either in evidence or documents that some of these units continued fighting, that would be wrong, would it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you are referring to when you say "fighting." If you think that that means going 50 metres further to take up a house that would be more safe, that would be stronger, that would provide greater visibility, then yes, there was fighting. However, if you believe that after the 10th streets and whole settlements were taken, then that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So it's a case of consolidation, perhaps consolidating in a stronger position, but no more; is that right? That's your evidence?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: The mere fact that they reached Milovo Brdo, the entire centre of the city and the bridges over the Vuka River and the timber market, that whole area was kept under firing control which means that they prevented the relocation of units. They prevented the replenishment and reinforcement of units. That is to say, at the time we believed that the fact that Milovo Brdo was reached meant that the town was split into two parts and all that remained for us to do is to wait for them to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What is the purpose of a daily briefing?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: At the daily briefing, every officer reports on the tasks carried out during the day, the problems he faced within his work, what sort of requests he had vis-a-vis the superior command in terms of resources, equipment, and so on and so forth, and what his proposals for future steps are or were. On the basis of that, the commanding officer running the briefing defines and issues tasks and takes any further measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that a briefing is not just a superior officer or a senior officer walking up and down with a clipboard issuing orders. That, of course, does play its part, but there is a give and take where there are questions and answers whether, for example, a target is achievable, whether logistics are sufficient to achieve an aim, issues of coordination. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: As company commanders, we proposed the activities for the upcoming days from the area of our competence. I was talking about the proposals. And the commander took decisions on the basis of our proposals and his conclusions and on the basis of the tasks conveyed to him by the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It doesn't really matter what - with the utmost of respect to them - what the superior command may actually order if units physically cannot do it. They perhaps will say they will do their best but if they cannot physically do it, that is one of the problems that can arise in a briefing. That's the purpose of briefings: To find out what is, to use your words, within your level of competence at that time. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat: At the start of the briefing, every commander reports on his matters. The commander, based on our proposals and the reports concerning our units, issues tasks. Once we receive our tasks, the tasks are no longer discussed. My duty as an officer is to carry out the task or to at least try to carry it out. And in case I'm unable to carry it out, my duty is to report to him about it. You know what the effect of insubordination is, of the refusal to carry out the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with that last part where in actual fact there may be a task and it is your duty to report to your superior officer that there may be difficulties in achieving that task. However, if he, having heard you, says you've still got to do it, you'd do it. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No, things weren't done at any cost. In other words, I tried to carry out the task. If I was unable to, then I informed the commander accordingly and the commander decided on the next steps to be taken. But to be going head over heels and causing the death of 10 to 15 men, this wasn't something that was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Let us now deal with an axis of attack. An axis of attack is perfectly obvious, but let us assume there are two units on that same axis of attack. One is TO, and another one is regular soldiers. Do you follow me so far?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If in actual fact there has been a briefing only for the regular soldiers, and there has been discussion about the level of competence of what can be achieved on that axis of attack, how is it then that the regular soldiers know what the problems will be from the TO or the TO know about the problems from the regular soldiers if you're not at the same briefing and under the same command?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Captain Radic advanced behind the Territorial Defence and behind Vujovic. He was able to see what was going on. My question to you is: Under the system prevailing at the time, would you expect for -- would you expect the person who completed I don't know what schools and has no military education at all and who is not familiar with the system at all to support you? Because an error in requesting support can cost lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, that leads to my next question: You were in charge of the mortar company, I think; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: It was called the mortar battery at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My apologies. And the function of a mortar battery often involves close support of ground troops; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: It is predominantly intended for close support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. There is an error in the transcript. There was a misinterpretation. Could my learned friend put the question again concerning Miroljub Vujovic. Because the text that can be read in the transcript, these are lines 17 to 22 were something else than what the witness said, but I would like my learned friend to check that. That was page 84, lines 18 to 22. I can tell you what the witness said but I don't want to. So perhaps my learned friend should put that question again as to what happens if two units are following the same axis of attack concerning artillery support.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think the problem is in the answer rather than the question. I didn't mention Vujovic at all; it was the witness who did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It appears, from Mr. Borovic's ear anyway, that there has been a mistranslation. Are you going to deal with the matter, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I wasn't going to deal with the matter. It can be dealt with in re-examination. The answer is there and it keeps disappearing off the screen as I speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Borovic, if you would be kind enough if you wish to deal with that matter when it comes up again in re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is not a great problem for the Defence or for re-examination but the sentence was translated differently because the answer said such people who have no education like Miroljub Vujovic could not request artillery support, and the answer as it is in the transcript is something quite different. It was important for me to point this out in order for my learned friend to know how things worked. Otherwise the matter becomes moot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. You've done your best to help Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, may I just try and find the question. We have managed to locate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask this question -- I'll read it because I certainly couldn't remember it. "If in actual fact there has been a briefing only for the regular soldiers, and there has been discussion about the level of competence of what can be achieved on that axis of attack, how is it, then, that the regular soldiers know what the problems will be from the TO or the TO know about the problems from the regular soldiers if they're not at the same briefing or under the same command?" Now, I've read that from the transcript, and I see Mr. Borovic is not happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are reading the wrong question. I gave you references. That was page 84, lines 18 to 22, where artillery support along the axis of attack is mentioned. If my learned friend doesn't wish to pursue this matter, as His Honour said, I'm perfectly content with the matter as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well I'm sorry, the reference that my learned friend gives is 18 to 22, and my 18 to 22 is an answer, not a question. Therefore, how can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Moore, I could give you the reference on our screen which is yet a third one. I'm sorry about that and the system but that is it. Now perhaps you might pay a little more attention to Mr. Borovic and identify the question on your screen and perhaps deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I have been paying attention to Mr. Borovic but he refers to an answer, not a question. May I try and glean what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. I was talking about the answer, because there is an error in the answer and not in the question, and that's for the third time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Right. The answer apparently -- let me read out what your answer is and then perhaps we can see if we can take it from there. "Captain Radic advanced behind the Territorial Defence and behind Vujovic. He was able to see what was going on. "My question to you is: Under the system prevailing at the time would you expect for -- would you expect the person who completed I don't know what schools and has no military education at all and who is not familiar with the system at all to support you because an error in requesting support can cost lives." Well, I'm sorry the answer, to me, makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you saying in that reply that in actual fact because a person was not educated, shall we say, overly, and had no military education at all, that he therefore would not be able to call in fire support for regular troops who were on the same axis of attack? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: The only officers who had the right to seek to call fire support were active-duty officers, namely commanders of companies and battalion commanders. At no point in time throughout the combat activities not -- I did not carry out a single combat action without receiving such calls from any other persons than company commanders and battalion commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So therefore what you are saying is as follows: That in actual fact if you had irregular and regular troops on the same axis of attack, it would be the regular officer who would coordinate the fire support. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: He detects targets of fire -- firing positions and issues the request to destroy them, and I'm talking about the active-duty officer. On the basis of the map of the town that we had, the officer would send such a request to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So - almost finished with the topic - if you had a TO separate briefing and a regular officer separate briefing that seems to be suggested by yourself and others, what I simply want to know is: How does one know what the other's goals are?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Major Tesic, who carried out the briefing with us, issued tasks and set out objectives. Most probably at a later stage, when issuing tasks to the Territorial Defence, he would adopt the tasks he issued to them with the task he -- tasks he had issued to me, in terms of fire support.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I am suggesting to you that if there is one person who knows about coordination and subordination and fire support, because it has to go through the regular officers, it will be Major Tesic; that is right isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: In essence, yes, he is the one who issues tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And therefore he is the one who will know whether units are subordinated to him, units under his control, isn't that right, and under the control of the companies?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you again: Within the composition of the 1st Motorised Battalion, the commander of which was Major Tesic, not a single unit was subordinated or attached, but Tesic also carried out the duty of commander of the assault detachment, if you get my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Then, quite simply, explain why Tesic should use the phrase: "I know that Radic's orders were fully complied with," if in actual fact these units were not subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Radic's orders to his troops and his company were fully complied with because that was the sort of officer he was. But Radic was not entitled to command the unit he was acting in coordination with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal then, please, with the fact that you said that you heard Tesic order Radic to the hospital on the 19th, so that you're familiar with the topic. Prior to speaking to myself, did you compile any document which you supplied to the Defence indicating that you had overheard this particular order?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't compile any document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So what are you using to remember an order 15 years ago where you said that the airwaves were being used 24 hours a day? Did you use a document?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I used my memory only. I remembered the important dates of certain events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would it surprise you to know that Major Tesic, in his interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, said that he did not issue any orders to Radic on the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that Tesic said that he didn't issue the order because I heard as much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
