utterances.text: But would it surprise you for Tesic to say that? "I saw Captain Radic in the hospital on the 19th of November. I did not issue him any orders relating to the evacuation of the hospital." Now, does that surprise you, bearing in mind what you've just said?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't believe that Major Tesic stated that. Therefore, this goes to show that it surprises me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In actual fact, paragraph 38, he says as follows: "On the 19th of November, there were members of the local Serb Vukovar TO in the hospital compound. I arrived at the hospital with a small number of men of the 1st Assault Group led by Sasa Bojkovski. Parts of the 3rd Assault Group of Captain Radic came from the flank, from the direction of the bus station. I had not issued orders to that effect to Radic." Now, you have told us the high regard that you hold Tesic in. So would you like to reflect upon your answer after 15 years of time elapse?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can -- I still hold Tesic in high esteem. He is the commander of the battalion I was waging a war with, or I served in in war. And I can't believe that he stated that. I don't know what to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, if you can't believe why he stated that, can I suggest one of the reasons that he stated it was because he said: "I did not issue him any orders relating to the evacuation of the hospital. That would have brought me into conflict with my commander since he had not issued orders to me." That was Mrksic. So he's saying he didn't get the orders from Mrksic and therefore he didn't order Radic. That was why. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: So you mean to say that after 49 days of war, during which no orders were refused, and after I and everyone else carried out Tesic's orders, someone on the 19th dared not to comply with his order or dared do something without an order from him. This was simply impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before we go on a break, as I presume, Your Honour, my learned friend is putting his questions carefully and that's all very well. However, at the end, he talks about Tesic's order concerning the 19th of November and refers to a part of Tesic's statement concerning the evacuation of the hospital and the order of -- on the evacuation of the hospital which did not take place on that day and has nothing to do with it. Because this is the order dated the 19th and the other the order dated the 20th. I believe in this way the witness is being misled. The question can stand without the reference to the evacuation of the hospital and then the witness can answer it. And I think my learned friend should put to him the question in this way, mentioning the evacuation of the hospital and the 19th. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, you have relied heavily upon a statement of a person that neither you have called nor is any Defence intending to call. You may, of course, properly put matters from that statement to the witness to see if the witness has a reaction. On a point, I think, different from the particular point Mr. Borovic has made but which has become apparent to the Chamber, you are by the end then using the answer as a point of argument to put to the witness. That, in the circumstances, in our view is taking the use you can make of that statement too far. Thank you. We will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vuckovic, you will be pleased to hear I've looked at all my questions to come, I have about 15 or 20 minutes, I think, and no more, and that may assist my learned friend with his next witness. Can I deal then, please, with the dinner that you say you had with Mr. Radic. I want to deal with that topic. Was the general intention to invite the officers, generally, to that dinner?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And presumably you were the focal point of the invitation from the local people. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Was I the one who decided which local people would be invited to the dinner? Is that what you want to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. What I really wanted to try and clarify - I'm not trying to catch you out in any way - is was it a dinner that was organised by local people, shall we say, to say thank you to the soldiers for liberating them, in general terms?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Local residents, yes. But only residents from the street where I was, which includes some seven to eight houses, meaning seven to eight families, not local residents of the entire settlement or anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And would it be right to say then again, in general terms, the officers were to be invited through you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And Major Tesic was invited; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Major Tesic wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But Major Tesic was there on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th, Major Tesic went to the command for a briefing or to report. Now you got me all -- yes, on the 20th, Major Tesic went to the command to submit a report, and I don't know when he came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That may well be the case. Are you saying Major Tesic was not in Vukovar on the 20th or he just was not around to go to the dinner?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Major Tesic was there for the beginning of the reporting and then went to the command. Captain Stijakovic completed the reporting and then issued tasks. Upon completion of the reporting, I called the officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, but my point is very simple. Here is what I will call a party, a dinner - take that back - a dinner organised in general terms by the civilians in your local area for the officers, and the one person I'd suggest who you're going to ask to come, even if he can't make it because of obligations, will be Major Tesic; he's your commanding officer. Now, he doesn't drink, you tell us he doesn't like drink, but he is the one person, I'd suggest, that you would invite. Now, I'm asking: Did you invite him?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Had he stayed until the end of the briefing, I would surely have invited him, just as I did invite Captain Stijakovic who thanked me for the invitation but said that he was unable to come because he had to stay at the command post where he had duties to attend to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How far away was Tesic's command post from where the dinner was being held?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: In my view, some 400 to 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can we assume that as there are 7-8 Motorolas, that we were not in party mode as such, that the Motorolas still remained with company commanders and people like Tesic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I think that that's not relevant or important because these things were not discussed on Motorolas. How could I call my commander, who had gone to the superior command, how could I call him on a Motorola and invite him to a dinner? That would be inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Well, we can deal with it a different way. I would suggest it is not inappropriate, perhaps, to contact Major Tesic because this clearly was an all-night affair. You could have contacted Major Tesic at 10.00 at night. The briefings in the command were over long before that, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know when he came back, and I really didn't pay attention to the time. We were sitting together in good company, in good mood, we were laughing, singing, so I simply wasn't paying attention to that. I considered everyone to be invited, and Major Tesic could have asked Captain Stijakovic. I don't even know whether they discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But are you saying that Tesic had gone for the command briefing to see Mrksic on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know with whom, but he definitely went to the command in Negoslavci. That's all I know. I don't know what was taking place in Negoslavci. But he went for a briefing to the brigade headquarters command. Every officer has his deputy and if he is absent, there are rules about substitution, just as Stijakovic substituted for Tesic when he was absent. The same applied to everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you see, we've heard evidence that Mr. Mrksic left his command because he was off to Belgrade to see his wife and the boiler was being heated up, so that was around about 7.30, 8.00. Did you ever check to see if Major Tesic was back and perhaps you could either contact him by Motorola, which you deem to be inappropriate, or send someone round, or indeed you personally go round and say: Look, we're having a dinner, would you like to come and join us?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't go anywhere from the house after coming back from the briefing. And if Colonel Mrksic went to Belgrade, Lieutenant-Colonel Panic was the one who briefed. That would be logical to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, never mind who's briefing. All I'm asking is: Did you or did you not contact Major Tesic, as an officer, to come and join you at the dinner? The answer is yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Because I didn't know at all when he came back, nor did I check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you have told us it was a long and enjoyable night which you felt, English phrase, a little rough the next day. Would that be right? A little fatigued?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you told Tesic on the 21st about the problems that you had had and the fact that you had been to the dinner?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because Tesic asked me why I had not been clean-shaven. We had been given an order that we can't have unkempt appearance, we had to look properly, so I was unshaven and rather dirty. My unit or, rather, some people from my unit were in the field where it was quite muddy, and the entire day we worked on my equipment pulling it out of the mud and so on. So as soon as he saw me, he said to me: Why do you look like this? This is improper. And Captain Stijakovic had already said that he had criticised me about it. So what he did was asked me about my dishevelled appearance and then I explained it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That your dishevelled appearance had been because had you stayed late or basically until the early hours of the morning and then had been busy working that day; is that right? That's why you had not shaved?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And since Major Tesic knew me really well, he was probably able to see on my face that I had partied hard last night. And since he absolutely cannot stand alcohol, he criticised me, he asked me who, when, where, and why, and then I explained it to him. I told him there was a dinner and this and that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There's a small problem, Mr. Vuckovic. Major Tesic wasn't in Vukovar on the 21st, he was in Belgrade, and he didn't come back to Vukovar until the 22nd. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he came back on the 21st in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I would suggest to you, regrettably, that you are a gentleman who has come to tell lies to help your friend and have been caught out. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the Judges' job is to establish whether I'm lying or not. I'm telling you what I know and what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When did you arrive in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: On Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who did you travel with?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: With Zirojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I thought you were going to say the airline, and I didn't mean it, it was an imprecise question. And what time did you come to the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly. I think at around 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's in the morning; yes?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think it's correct to say, as indeed you're entitled, you saw Defence lawyers. Did you see them on Saturday?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: At what time did you see the Defence lawyers, approximately, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in the afternoon, towards the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And which lawyers did you see, can you remember the name, male or female? And Mr. Borovic wins on this one, I think.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I met with Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And at what time did you see Mr. Borovic and for how long?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly. I saw him on Saturday towards the evening. In the evening we were together for an hour, hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did Mr. Borovic make notes of what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I think so. We talked. I don't know what he noted down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you see Mr. Borovic again on Sunday or did you see the ladies on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Mira was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic, as we know her.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And at what time did you see her?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think it was 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how long did the conversations last with the lawyers on Sunday?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately, again, hour to hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And was that the last time you saw the lawyers or had contact with the lawyers? And please reflect upon your answer.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I think that we had a coffee together yesterday, or rather last night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And who did you have a coffee with?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: With Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And anyone else?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Forca was present last night as well, whom I happen to know professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Who will be our next witness; is that right? You may know that, you may not.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I, at the very start, reminded you, although I'm sure you remember it, that we met in Belgrade. I want to deal with that, if I may, briefly. You saw me along with an interpreter and an investigator at the offices of the Tribunal in Belgrade. That's right, I think, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the format was that the -- I think there were introductions, the investigator read out some prepared form about taking a statement, and you were asked whether you had received a waiver. Now, do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And isn't it right to say that you said that you had not received a waiver?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When did you actually receive the waiver? Because we have heard evidence the waiver was issued on the 13th of September.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I explained it to you back then. I said that around the 22nd of August I was on vacation and I returned from my vacation on the 18th of September. Upon returning to work, I received a call from my chief, my superior officer, who handed me in the appropriate paperwork. That is to say, that during my vacation, nobody contacted me, nobody called me to tell me to come in so that I can receive the waiver. Before going on my vacation, I received a notice to attend the interview with you. I signed the receipt which was sent to you. I came to see you at the set time, and I said to you all of these things during our interview. I received the waiver on the 18th, and our interview was on the 14th of September. And I apologise, that can be verified with my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when were you informed that in actual fact you were being asked to see officers from the Prosecution? We know you attended on the 14th. When did you receive notification that you were going to be spoken to?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Just before going on my vacation, in mid-August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal with just two other matters. I will suggest it to you, because I think it's only fair and right. There may or may not have been a dinner on the night of the 20th, but I would suggest to you that in actual fact Captain Radic left much earlier than you said and had left somewhere between 11.00 p.m. and 1.00 a.m. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I stand by my statement. I know how this transpired because it was taking place in the house where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Finally this: Did company commanders, did they have a soldier who escorted them, what I would call a quasi body-guard? When they were serving in Vukovar, obviously.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did, but in the very beginning. We are now speaking of the beginning of October, up until the 9th or 10th or at around that time. Because at that time, we were still not sufficiently familiar with the streets. There were many ruins, and it was unsafe, generally. However, as soon as we consolidated our lines, as soon as the fire system was established, there was no need for that any longer and, among other things, the battalion commander, Major Tesic, had ordered that all movement be reduced to minimum. At night, we were banned from any movement except from the observation post to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Zirojevic, who was the previous witness, said that he attended your dinner, that -- no, it's my fault, it's Mr. Radic said that he went to your dinner, acquired some cigarettes and took them across to yourself and your soldier. What is the name of that soldier whom you were with and that he referred to?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't bring it just to me and my soldier. I had a total of seven soldiers with me, not just one. I remember the names of some of them. One of them was called Nikola Kaludjerski, the other one was Mirko Ilic, and then Mehmedovic or something like that, and I don't remember the names of others, I just remember their faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why should he merely refer to singular, a soldier, rather than soldiers? Who might that be if he's just referring to one person?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how four or five or six cartons of cigarettes can be given to just one soldier. What is one soldier going to do with that? What about all the other soldiers? What are they to do? The cigarettes were given to the troops and they were on the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you are saying that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sorry, my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My learned friend, just to avoid any confusion, there was no mention of one soldier, and my learned friend can verify this if he wishes to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, my recollection it was a soldier, singular, unnamed, and I merely inquire whether -- what the name was. Your Honour, I can assist the Court if Your Honour would give me one moment. Just reading back at 12.664/23, this is Mr. Radic: "I still had some cartons of cigarettes left there, and I grabbed one of those to take back to the Second Lieutenant Vuckovic and his soldier."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I'm just asking who your soldier is, not plural.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you, first of all, Radic never saw me at the observation post with less than four soldiers. That is to say, during operations, I always had four soldiers around me; two who were dealing with communications, and two who were scouts, by specialty. So it cannot possibly be that I had just one soldier with me. In town, if I can say so, or at the observation point in Oslobodjenje Street, there were a total of seven soldiers with me. The rest of the unit was at the firing position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if Radic says that he's wrong. You don't have a soldier?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was always in the company of several soldiers. And I'm not talking about escorts. I'm talking about the work at the observation post and I had several posts. My main observation post was in the Oslobodjenje Street and I went there every night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on page 12.236, this isn't what it says on that page. I wasn't able to locate it anywhere. And in the notes that I made, it says "soldiers" which arises logically from the answer. But at any rate, I believe the witness has answered this question on several times. If my learned friend wishes to insist upon this matter, he should find the page and the relevant lines where it was stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've given the reference and I'm not going to repeat it. I certainly have got a printing, a printout of the examination-in-chief. I don't know if there are two translations or not. I certainly have singular soldier. That's all I can say. And I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Yes, in the English version, Mr. Borovic, it is "soldier" in the singular. Now, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our notes, which we didn't know that they were going to be used anywhere, it says "soldiers." It may have been misinterpretation. But on the basis of the witness's answers, the matter is quite clear, and I will accept any decision by the Trial Chamber in this regard. Thank you. If Mr. Moore has finished, I would like to start my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuckovic, do you know that Mr. Radic was given the medal of honour?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he received the medal because he saved your life on two occasions or because of the military activities in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: He received the medal for the totality of the activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In proofing you, did I speak to you on a separate occasion and did I speak to Mr. Zirojevic separately?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: As the Prosecutor put to you Borivoje Tesic's statement on several occasions and he did not present to you paragraph 48, I will put it to you. To the question from the OTP whether he had seen Radic on the 20th of November, his answer was as follows: "I saw Radic on that day, on the 20th of November in the evening." He went on to say: "The commander of my mortar company told me later on that Radic" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the form of the question. Mr. Borovic is merely trying to give evidence as such and not elicit an answer by way of re-examination. It is to the form that I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm afraid Mr. Borovic may be learning bad habits, Mr. Moore. He is following very much the form that you used persistently in your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm not taking this against Mr. Moore. We are complementing each other. "The commander of my mortar company told me later on that Radic had stayed on with him on the 20th of November, 1991, late into the night." Tesic gave the statement to the OTP investigators in 2003. Is this consistent with what I asked you, whether you spoke to Tesic on that evening?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said that you heard from Radic that Tesic visited him -- his company only once during these combat activities. Do you have any such knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was never at my observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: From the 10th to the 18th of November, who was the commander of Assault Detachment 1?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Major Borivoje Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From the 10th of November to -- through to the fall of Vukovar, under whose control were the TO Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica detachment?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: They were within Assault Detachment 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Under whose control therefore?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Major Tesic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor asked you about the reason why Tesic stated many matters differently because --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Defence counsel please repeat the last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If I'm telling that you these are the reasons, do you think that I am right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Now that I look back at things, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You were an artillery soldier?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: I am still.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Are the rules governing infantry different?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, drastically different.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And that means?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: That means that an infantry officer cannot directly control an artillery unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Borivoje Tesic gave his statement to the OTP in 2003. Would you be surprised if I told you that in 2004 Sasa Bojkovski gave a statement to the same OTP and he, in answering the question as to where he was on the 19th of November when the captured soldiers were released, in paragraph 23 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... perhaps that's a different issue. I have not referred to Bojkovski's statement in any way at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, I'm trying to discern what the point of the statement is that's relevant for -- or arises from cross-examination, Mr. Borovic. Can you tell me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Openly and briefly, the -- Bojkovski was the person who Tesic ordered to provide military security for the hospital on the 19th of November, and Bojkovski in his statement to the OTP in 2004 says: "I didn't have any orders concerning the visit to the hospital." The Prosecutor made -- mentioned Bojkovski on page 10 concerning this order -- or, rather, I apologise, on page 95 -- or rather -- on page 35, not -- and page 90.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you be surprised if I told you that he didn't have the order to secure the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I still haven't seen, Mr. Borovic, how this arises out of cross-examination. I know it's late in the day and I'm probably slow, but I still haven't got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness was told that Tesic claimed that on the 19th of November, he did not issue Radic with any orders concerning external security of the hospital. The witness stated that he heard the order issued over the Motorola. He was also given Tesic's statement about giving this order to Bojkovski, and I'm reading here Bojkovski stated in the statement that he didn't have an order to that effect and that's all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note again that a question and answer were not interpreted because the interpreter didn't catch the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are all three still not able to see that this arises out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that the witness's explanation of the order was sufficient. I do not wish to waste any more time. I simply wanted to put to the witness that Sasa Bojkovski never had the order to provide security to the hospital by following the way in which my learned friend did it. If this is not re-examination proper, then we can let the matter stand where they are. Or once again, briefly, it was put to the witness that Tesic issued the order to provide security for the hospital to Sasa Bojkovski, and I presented the witness with Bojkovski's statement where Bojkovski stated that he didn't have any such orders. Bojkovski gave his statement one year after Tesic did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Borovic, you've battled strongly but you may have to accept defeat. We're still not able to see it as a matter arising.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can afford one defeat a day. I have the following question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is there a Serb news agency who prepares witnesses for testimony before this Court?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR VUCKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have completed my re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will be pleased to know, sir, that that concludes the evidence that you will be asked to give here. We would thank you for your attendance and for the assistance that you've been able to give. You are, of course, now, at liberty to return to your ordinary activities. Thank you again, and the court officer will show you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is becoming a habit with witness after another, we've finished with about 10 or 12 minutes today to go. Is there any point in bringing the witness in and swearing him in, Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is called efficient work on the part of the Defence. And I would request that we ask the examination -- that we start the examination of the expert witness tomorrow morning. We would also tender 92 bis witness statements into evidence. It would take only five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you do that, while we still have our mind on the expert witness, what would be your expectation of the time that witness will take?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, having heard your decision concerning the Defence for Mr. Sljivancanin, my intention was to shorten the testimony. However, I would like to give the opportunity to my colleagues to examine Mr. Forca in detail. I do believe that we would be able to finish his examination tomorrow, perhaps we would need to use up some time on Thursday as well, but it will be depend entirely upon my learned friend opposite. We hope to finish tomorrow and possibly we will need some time on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When you say "we," is that including your friend opposite?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do believe that we cooperated well and are doing the same job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: All right. That's not just an estimate of the Defence evidence but of all evidence of the witness. Very well. Does any other counsel have any different view of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if my learned friend would be able to estimate, and I don't attempt to tie him down in any way, but how long does he anticipate that he will actually be in chief and whether in actual fact the Defence on behalf of Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Sljivancanin, how long they might be? Because that gives a much better time estimate for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While you're on your feet, how do you see your cross-examination at the moment, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, actually, it's Mr. Weiner's cross-examination, so -- but we are indivisible. So I would have thought that we would take no more than, I would have thought, three to four hours. It just really depends how -- how long and what issues Mr. Forca deals with. I can see it being a lot shorter. That would be our intention, to have it shorter. But until we actually know what issues are going to be dealt with, it's rather difficult to estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, do you have any expectation of cross-examining tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How long do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My examination should not take longer than an hour. If all of us invested additional effort to finish tomorrow, I would be able to shorten it down to 30 or 40 minutes to the very relevant if all the others would do the same, but if the Prosecution requires three to four hours, then I really don't see the possibility of finishing tomorrow, and therefore I don't see the point of me shortening my cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Oh, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will be examining Mr. Forca. On the basis of what was said, I estimate our cross-examination of the witness would last about 45 minutes, it could be less, but not more than 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, even if Mr. Moore is at the lower end of his estimate, I think we are likely to creep into Thursday, by the sound of everything put together, although we do have a full day tomorrow, so we live in hope. Now, Mr. Borovic, you promised us the prospect of some exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're right. My colleague Tapuskovic has just completed the filing. Perhaps we could leave that for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as we promised, our motion is being translated and we will do it in writing after all because the witnesses on our exhibit list, and there is 41 of them who were not tendered through the witnesses we called so far, we will give an explanation as to why we believe that they have to be admitted into evidence. The motion will be officially filed tomorrow. We believe that before the testimony of our military expert, Mr. Forca, we should use up three or four minutes to move that two 92 bis witness statements be admitted into evidence. Your decision was of a provisional nature because the witness statements had to be accompanied by 92 bis certifications which were formerly certified by the Registrar, and we would need to discuss this matter tomorrow for -- briefly for only two to three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it that you need those statements for the expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I will remind you, 92 bis statements go to the character of the accused and are in no way linked to the testimony of the expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That being the case, it may be that we should go straight to the expert witness and deal with your formal written motion when we have finished with the expert witness. That, in particular, would give an opportunity to the other parties to see the document before it's raised. It's not to be filed until tomorrow, it may be a cause of unnecessary delay if they've not had a chance to look at it. We will, therefore, unless there's some need for those statements for the last witness, we would, I think, prefer to leave it until after the witness's evidence has been dealt with and it may be possible that that can be all accomplished in the course of tomorrow. We will live in that hope. Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is the way we will proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And we will adjourn now and resume again tomorrow at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 18th day of October, 2006, at 9.30 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.57 p.m.,
